title: Executable FinMR: Arelle-Based Symbolic Baselines and an Executability Audit for XBRL Mathematical Reasoning

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The stated purpose is to provide a strong symbolic baseline for the FinMR XBRL reasoning benchmark to test whether it measures reasoning or XBRL tooling. Paper [7] ("RE-IMAGINE") introduces a framework to evaluate reasoning benchmarks and distinguish reasoning ability from statistical recall, which aligns with the objective of testing benchmark validity. Paper [10] ("Benchmark^2") also focuses on evaluating benchmark quality, including discriminability and ranking consistency, which overlaps with the goal of assessing whether FinMR measures reasoning. Both papers share the same problem-class objective of evaluating benchmark validity, making the purpose covered.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves an Arelle-based symbolic baseline that reconstructs executable XBRL packages from benchmark queries and computes answers using standards-compliant DQC rule semantics. Paper [5] ("Using SPIN to Formalise XBRL Accounting Regulations on the Semantic Web") formalizes XBRL accounting regulations using semantic web technologies, which includes rule-based reasoning over XBRL data. Paper [11] ("Towards a Framework for Writing Executable Natural Language Rules") discusses executable rules for reasoning tasks, which overlaps with the reconstruction and execution of XBRL packages. Both papers use rule-based symbolic reasoning primitives applied to XBRL, making the mechanism covered.

### Evaluation
The evaluation reports accuracy on the FinMR benchmark and compares it against LLM baselines. Paper [7] ("RE-IMAGINE") uses a systematic evaluation pipeline for reasoning benchmarks, including accuracy comparisons across models, which matches the evaluation design. Paper [10] ("Benchmark^2") also evaluates benchmarks systematically using metrics like discriminability and ranking consistency, which aligns with the comparative evaluation of FinMR. Both papers use comparable evaluation designs, making the evaluation covered.

### Domain
The domain is financial numerical reasoning over XBRL filings. Paper [4] ("Standardisert elektronisk regnskapsrapportering i Norge") discusses XBRL-based financial reporting, which is the same general application area. Paper [18] ("Xbrl") also focuses on XBRL applications in financial reporting, further confirming domain coverage. Both papers address financial reasoning within the XBRL framework, making the domain covered.

**PURPOSE: Provide a strong symbolic baseline for the FinMR XBRL reasoning benchmark to test whether it measures reasoning or XBRL tooling.**

The purpose is specifically to probe whether a benchmark measures genuine reasoning vs. tooling/artifact exploitation, by constructing a symbolic baseline that outperforms LLMs. Papers [28] and [29] are about partial-input baselines to diagnose whether datasets are "cheatable" — [29] explicitly uses "hypothesis-only baselines" to show NLI datasets have artifacts, and [28] discusses "partial-input baselines" to assess dataset difficulty. The underlying objective — build a strong non-reasoning baseline to test whether a benchmark actually measures what it claims — is substantively equivalent. Paper [12] also introduces "functional benchmarks" to test whether models reason or recall, and measures a "reasoning gap." However, [28]/[29] most directly match: constructing a strong baseline to reveal that a benchmark can be solved without the intended capability.

**MECHANISM: Arelle-based symbolic baseline with href rewriting, linkbaseRef injection, truncated-XML repair, and DQC rule semantics.**

This is a highly specific technical primitive: using a standards-compliant XBRL processor (Arelle) with DQC validation rules, plus XML repair/reconstruction steps, to compute answers deterministically. Paper [5] discusses formalizing XBRL accounting regulations using SPIN on the Semantic Web — related to rule-based XBRL reasoning but not the same primitive (no Arelle, no DQC rules, no XML reconstruction). Paper [9] discusses hard/soft rules for XBRL but is descriptive, not a computational baseline mechanism. Paper [11] discusses executable natural language rules. None of the prior papers describe the specific primitive of reconstructing XBRL packages from benchmark queries and applying DQC rule semantics via a standards-compliant processor. This mechanism is genuinely absent.

**EVALUATION: 42.17% accuracy on 332-instance set, 71.79% on executable subset, vs. LLM baselines.**

The evaluation design is: run a symbolic/rule-based system on a benchmark, compare accuracy against LLM baselines. This design — comparing a symbolic/rule-based approach against LLMs on a reasoning benchmark using accuracy metrics — appears in papers like [3] (FinChain compares symbolic vs. neural approaches), [1] (FinRule-Bench evaluates LLMs on financial reasoning), and [13] (neuro-symbolic benchmark suite comparing approaches). The design of "accuracy on benchmark instances, broken down by subset, compared to LLM baselines" is a standard evaluation design present in multiple prior papers. Paper [1] uses accuracy metrics comparing LLMs on financial reasoning benchmarks. This evaluation design is covered.

**DOMAIN: Financial numerical reasoning over XBRL filings (symbolic/neuro-symbolic).**

Papers [1], [3], [24], [25] all work in financial reasoning/analysis. Papers [2], [4], [5], [6], [8], [9], [17], [18], [20] all work specifically with XBRL filings. The domain of financial reasoning over XBRL is clearly covered by multiple prior papers.

**PURPOSE: Diagnose why a benchmark is hard by auditing whether its instances are even executable.**

The purpose is to audit benchmark instance executability to understand why a benchmark is difficult — essentially a benchmark quality/validity audit focused on runnability of instances. Paper [20] "Quality Benchmarking of Datasets Used in Software Effort Estimation" addresses data quality problems in benchmarks (noise, outliers, incompleteness). Paper [9] "Evaluating Benchmark Quality: a Mutation-Testing-Based Methodology" addresses benchmark quality evaluation. However, neither specifically targets *executability* of instances as the diagnostic lens — they focus on data quality in a different sense. Paper [16] "ANGHABENCH: A Suite with One Million Compilable C Benchmarks" specifically addresses compilability (a form of executability) of benchmark instances, noting that "the availability of human-made benchmarks is limited" and that synthesized code differs from actual programs — it explicitly curates *compilable* benchmarks, which is substantively equivalent to auditing whether benchmark instances are executable. The purpose of ensuring/auditing that benchmark instances are actually runnable/compilable is the same underlying objective.

**MECHANISM: Executability audit classifying instances as executable or assigning failure labels; failure taxonomy over non-executable instances.**

Paper [16] ANGHABENCH mines compilable C benchmarks and classifies programs by compilability — this is structurally equivalent to classifying instances as executable vs. non-executable. Paper [18] "Common Errors of XBRL Implementation" classifies XBRL errors/failures. Paper [6] "On Classification in the Study of Failure, and a Challenge to Classifiers" addresses failure classification taxonomies. Paper [14] "Taxonomy of Transport Layer Security (TLS) Revocation Failure Scenarios" builds a failure taxonomy. The combination of executability classification + failure taxonomy is partially covered: [16] covers the executability classification aspect, and [6]/[14] cover failure taxonomy construction. Paper [18] specifically covers XBRL error classification. The mechanism of classifying instances as executable/non-executable and building a failure taxonomy is covered by [16] (executability classification) and [6] (failure taxonomy).

**EVALUATION: 58.73% executability rate, specific failure breakdown percentages.**

These are specific empirical findings/measurements, not an evaluation design. The evaluation design here is essentially: run a tool (Arelle) on each instance, record pass/fail, categorize failures, report percentages. This is a standard audit/classification protocol. Paper [20] uses dataset quality auditing with similar counting/categorization methodology. Paper [16] reports compilability rates across a corpus. The evaluation design (run instances through a validator, count pass/fail, categorize failures) is a standard audit protocol seen in [16] and [20]. The specific numbers are findings, not design elements.

**DOMAIN: Benchmark quality auditing (XBRL artifacts).**

XBRL is addressed in papers [7], [8], [10], [12], [15], [18], [19 - FinAuditing]. Paper [8] "FinAuditing" explicitly works with XBRL benchmarks for LLM evaluation. Benchmark quality auditing appears in [9], [20]. The combination of XBRL + benchmark auditing is covered by [8] (XBRL benchmark) and [9]/[20] (benchmark quality). The domain of XBRL artifacts is covered by [8], and benchmark quality auditing is covered by [9]/[20].
